claims.text: In situ substrate preheating during additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi mitigates residual thermal stresses relative to room-temperature builds.
In situ substrate preheating improves the mechanical performance of additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi relative to room-temperature builds.
The intervention is applicable to laser powder-bed fusion of miniature AlCrFeNiSi components with sub-centimeter features in an inert atmosphere.
Substrate preheating moderates the thermal gradient during fabrication.
A moderated thermal gradient produces more uniform solidification.
More uniform solidification produces a refined microstructure.
More uniform solidification produces a less defect-prone microstructure.
Substrate preheating reduces the temperature differential between the melt pool and the underlying material.
Reducing the melt-pool-to-substrate temperature differential lowers cooling rates.
Reducing the melt-pool-to-substrate temperature differential lowers thermal contraction.
The controlled thermal profile limits residual-stress formation.
The controlled thermal profile minimizes microstructural defects.
Preheated components will have greater ductility than components made under conventional high-thermal-load conditions.
Preheated components will have greater strength than components made under conventional high-thermal-load conditions.
Conventional room-temperature additive-manufacturing builds typically exhibit high thermal gradients.
Conventional room-temperature additive-manufacturing builds typically exhibit significant residual stresses.
Conventional room-temperature additive-manufacturing builds typically exhibit compromised mechanical properties.
The effectiveness of substrate preheating may depend on layer thickness, preheating temperature, and component geometry.
